fatal_errors: The proposed W addition does not reconstruct the target comparison between CrFeTaVW and Ta-to-Ti-substituted CrFeTiVW, including mechanical alloying, SPS consolidation, and MD versus hybrid MD/MC analysis.
No controlled falsification experiment is supplied, despite the explicit requirement to test both the performance prediction and the proposed mechanism.

Formation of fine, coherent W-rich precipitates is asserted without thermodynamic, crystallographic, or cited experimental support; minor W could instead remain in BCC solid solution or form incoherent segregation.

The prediction that W addition will preserve roughly 40% ductility and avoid degrading thermal transport is unsupported. The cited evidence does not test W-modified TiVNbTa, precipitation, conductivity, or interfacial heat-transfer performance.

Temperature, W concentration, heat treatment, strain rate, loading mode, and quantitative thermal-transport limits are not specified, making the approximately 500 MPa strength prediction non-falsifiable as written.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad engineering problem of improving TiVNbTa high-temperature strength while retaining heat-transfer capability, and it correctly states much of the reported TiVNbTa strength baseline. It is nevertheless disconnected from the hidden target, which concerns CrFeTaVW/CrFeTiVW processing, phase constitution, segregation, thermal diffusivity, and hybrid MD/MC predictions. Even as an alternative hypothesis, its central causal chain is weakly supported: E1 concerns the unmodified NbTaTiV alloy and does not establish W-rich coherent precipitation, while E2 only provides general fusion-material requirements. The numerical strength target, retained 40% ductility, and unchanged thermal conductivity are speculative. The absence of a composition series, matched processing controls, microscopy/diffraction tests of precipitate coherency, thermal-diffusivity measurements, and high-temperature mechanical tests prevents discrimination between precipitation strengthening, solid-solution strengthening, and ordinary segregation.
